summary: Describes five types of SNMP applications that use an SNMP engine: command generators, command responders, notification originators, notification receivers and proxy forwarders. It also defines MIB modules for targets, notification filtering and proxy forwarding. It replaces RFC 2263 and was replaced by RFC 2573.

eli5.summary: It lists the five kinds of jobs in an SNMP system. This version replaced an earlier one and was then replaced itself.

questions: what are the five snmp application types
when should i use trap vs inform
subtitle: Defines five types of SNMP applications and their messaging behavior.

tldr.problem: SNMPv3 systems need standard patterns for how different types of SNMP applications work, from sending commands to receiving notifications to forwarding messages.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies five application types: command generators that initiate requests, command responders that handle them, notification originators that send alerts, notification receivers that handle them, and proxy forwarders that relay messages between systems.
tldr.outcome: This became the foundation for SNMPv3 agent implementations, though it was quickly obsoleted by RFC 2573 with clarifications and corrections.

facts.label: Application types
facts.value: 5 (command generators, responders, notification originators, receivers, proxy forwarders)

today: RFC 2273 was obsoleted by RFC 2573 in September 1998. The newer version clarified several definitions and corrected some SNMP module number assignments, but the five application types and their procedures remain the same in SNMPv3.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2273 defines the five types of SNMP applications that work with an SNMP engine. An SNMP application is software that uses the SNMP protocol to send or receive management messages. Each type has a different role:

  • Command generators send SNMP requests (Get, GetNext, GetBulk, Set) and process responses.
  • Command responders listen for requests, perform the requested operation on managed objects, and send back responses.
  • Notification originators monitor a system for events and send SNMP notifications (Trap or Inform messages) when events occur.
  • Notification receivers listen for incoming notifications and respond to Inform messages.
  • Proxy forwarders relay requests, responses, and notifications between different SNMP systems or versions.

The RFC also defines three MIB modules that provide configuration tables for management targets, notification filtering, and proxy rules.
sections.eli5: Imagine a network management center that monitors equipment. Some programs ask questions, some answer them, some send alerts, some listen for alerts, and some pass messages around. This RFC explains how each type should work.

sections.title: Management Targets and SNMP Parameters
sections.content:
A management target is the configuration for how to send a message to a destination. It combines two pieces of information:

  • Destination information: the transport domain (such as UDP/IP) and the transport address (IP address and port).
  • SNMP parameters: the message processing model (SNMP version), security model, security level, and security name (the user or principal being used).

Command generators and notification originators must look up or be configured with management targets to know where and how to send their messages. Proxy forwarders translate incoming management target information into outgoing target information to determine where to forward messages. The SNMP-TARGET-MIB module provides tables for storing and managing this configuration.
sections.eli5: A management target is like an address label: it says where to send a message, who sent it, and what kind of security to use.

sections.title: Request and Response Procedures
sections.content:
Command generator applications use a sendPdu interface to send requests to the SNMP engine. The request includes the transport details, the SNMP version and security settings, the context (which engine and which managed object collection), and the PDU itself. The engine returns a handle that the application can use to match an incoming response.

When a response arrives, the command generator must verify that all the parameters match the original request and that the request-id is correct. Only then does it process the response.

Command responder applications register with the SNMP engine for the request types they handle. When a request arrives, the responder determines whether the requestor has access to the requested objects (using the security name, security level, and context). If allowed, it performs the management operation and sends a response. If not, it sends an error.
sections.eli5: When one program asks for information, it sends a request and waits for a response. The program that answers checks whether the requestor is allowed to know the answer, then sends it back or says no.

sections.title: Notifications and Alarms
sections.content:
Notification originator applications send Trap messages (one-way notifications) or Inform messages (notifications that request a response). Before sending, the originator determines:

  • Which management targets should receive the notification.
  • For each target, whether to send a Trap (no response expected) or an Inform (response expected, with retries if needed).
  • Whether the notification passes any filtering rules and whether the requestor has access to see the managed objects being reported.

Notification receiver applications register to listen for both Trap and Inform PDU types. When a Trap arrives, the receiver simply extracts and processes it. When an Inform arrives, the receiver sends back a Response PDU with a matching request-id.
sections.eli5: One program can notice when something important happens and send an alarm message to other programs. Some alarms are one-way shouts, others expect the listener to say they got it.

sections.title: Proxy Forwarding
sections.content:
Proxy forwarders act as intermediaries that relay SNMP messages without interpreting them. They forward four types of messages:

  • Requests: Forward Get, GetNext, GetBulk, or Set requests to another SNMP engine, then forward the response back to the original requester.
  • Notifications: Forward Trap and Inform notifications to configured destinations, and for Informs, forward responses back to the original notification originator.
  • Responses: Deliver responses to requests that the proxy previously forwarded.
  • Report indications: Deliver error reports for previously forwarded messages.

The key difference between a proxy and a command responder is that a proxy does not interpret the requested managed objects. It simply translates the incoming management target (who is asking, from where, with what security) into an outgoing management target (where to forward it, with what security) and relays the message. This allows proxies to work across different SNMP versions and transport types without knowing the MIB structure.
sections.eli5: A proxy is like a mail carrier who forwards packages to the right address without opening them. It just needs to know the translation rule: this kind of request goes to that machine.
